_MSVMCU0903_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ ### MARKET DEVELOPMENTS _Copper edges up during March under generally

supportive macro economic and industry data_ _LME copper stocks reverse the three-month climb…_ _..and then the new US Treasury scheme encourages further price gains in metals generally_ _Market ignored the latest gloomy figures from the ICSG…_ Copper prices generally edged up during March, thereby continuing the mildly bullish trend set in motion during the final week of February. In fact, the _lowest_ price ($3355/t – 3-month LME) came on the first trading day of the month (2nd ), which was little more than a mild correction due to profit-taking following a $110/t hike over the prior week. Prices continued to build from there for the next five days and ended up at $3725/t by the 6th . A steady week saw 3m quotes level out in that range through to the 16th , but since then prices track higher under generally supportive macro economic news and pertinent copper data. By the 23rd , copper had hit its high for the month by breaking through the $4000/t barrier for the first time since November 10th last year, reaching $4045/t. This provided an opportunity for more profit-taking on the 24-25th , and prices slipped back to the $3950/t range. Behind the price strength during the first half of the month lay virtually daily withdrawals of stock on the LME. In our last report, we noted how LME stocks had surged from a year-opening 342kt to almost 550kt by February 24th . Over the course of the next three weeks, however, LME material fell away to around 490kt. As we go to press, LME stocks have edged back over the 0.5Mt mark once again, but copper prices (as with the metals complex generally) ignored that bearish move and focused instead on the new US-government sponsored plan released on March 23rd . Under the scheme, the US government would provide up to $100Bn to private investors to buy toxic real estate-related assets from the banks, supported by debt guarantees. This would transfer the responsibility of assessing a value of those assets from the US Treasury across to the private sector, with the aim being to encourage a speedier resolution to what is one of the key structural financial problems in the US. Equally ignored during the final full week of the month was the latest release from the International Copper Study Group (ICSG), which focused on the market surplus that had built up during the second half of last year. According to the ICSG, demand was down in all the main consuming areas of the world (c.9% in the USA, over 4% in Western Europe, and by 5.4% in Japan), with only the CIS (+5.4%) and China (+14.2%) enabling global copper demand to record growth of just 2.2% year on year. The ICSG’s year-end surplus estimate came to 363kt. **MONTHLY INDEXED LME CASH METAL PRICES (January 2007 = 100)** Price Index 2nd Jan 2008=100

_March 2009_ _Page 2_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ But in this final week of March, arguably all the attention was of where the market was headed next, not where it was nearly three months ago, and for the first time in a while, the market was looking bullish. Lower stocks and higher prices aside, there were other reasons to feel optimistic. For example, the SRB’s purchases were still in the news, even if we knew little more than a month ago about the Bureau’s intentions, and this month, as expected, this translated into higher product premia. European premia strengthened for the first time since May last year. Unfortunately the firmer rates reflected Chinese buying rather than any pick up in _fresh_ European demand. Chinese consumers, traders and the SRB have been keen purchasers of LME material in recent weeks because of the favourable LME/SHFE arbitrage where Shanghai prices have traded at a premium to LME quotes throughout the month. Thus several large European market participants are reported to have shipped material to China where a much higher premium could be achieved. Low freight rates to China, currently as little as $10/t, were also an influencing factor. As a consequence, premia for Chilean and Grade A cathode from Rotterdam traded at $40-50/t, up from $2040/t in February and $10-30/t in January. Warrants from Italian locations also fetched between $40-50/t, up $10/t from the previous month. Likewise the price for standard grade material also increased by $10/t, up from -$30/t to - $10/t in February to -$20/t to level currently. Increased tightness in scrap availability was mainly responsible for this latter rise. Meanwhile in China itself, premia rose steadily during the month, up from $110/t in February to a peak of $150/t. The increase reflected a tighter supply of intermediates, as well as the ongoing tightness in scrap availability, and the favourable LME/SHFE price arbitrage. As noted, Shanghai prices continued to trade at a premium to LME quotes during the month. During March SHFE quotes, on a comparable basis (i.e net of VAT) as of the 24th , averaged $164/t above LME prices. This followed an average price arbitrage of $222/t in February and $214/t in January and should lead to further increases in net refined imports through to April. Latest trade data showed that net refined copper imports during the first two months of the year increased by a staggering 71.5% (+187kt) year on year. However, as we discuss at length in the Consumption section, some of this increase in refined imports must already be feeding through into the SRB’s stockpiling requirements, as not all is being converted into end-user demand. _..as it focused on where the market is headed next_ _European premia rise under strong Chinese buying_ _Chinese premia also rise under tight scrap and a favourable arbitrage_

_March 2009_ _Page 3_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ _US premia unchanged under low demand conditions…_ _..but some from the financial sector are beginning to believe that we have hit bottom…_ _..and this may bring the funds back to commodities…_ _..as some investors indicate a will to re-invest_ Finally, in the US very little spot business was reported during the month as consumers remained well covered for their Q1 commitments - and probably beyond. Producers and consumers there still note the poor level of business going forward, with Asarco making shift changes at its rod and cake plants that suggest that the market remains down by as much as 20% on previously expected levels. As noted in our January monthly report many US consumers carried inventory over from the fourth quarter last year. Thus US premia continued to trade between 3.5c/lb and 4.5c/lb. While there is little debate about the ongoing constraints on demand generally, there has been some air of optimism during March that we have not detected for some time. With some macro economic analysts believing we have “reached the bottom”, the question will be if more influential players can be dragged along, and by this we mean the funds. Most of the funds we have spoken with recently still say that there is no real improvement in sight, and that they continue to look for that renewal of confidence before they take another meaningful sortie into the commodities sector. Going forward, we believe that investors will retain their interest in commodity markets. Although passive, long only, index-based strategies are less attractive in the current environment, increased volatility can benefit investors adopting short term strategies such as those used by CTAs. Similarly once the economy stabilises and the first signs of growth emerge, exchange traded products (ETP), also know as Exchange Traded Funds (ETF), will provide investors with a straight forward means of gaining exposure to commodities that have a positive, fundamentally based price outlook. However, unlike the last upswing in commodity prices where the impact of investors was amplified through the use of leverage, the difficulties in securing credit and the more stringent management of risk is likely to diminish the impact of investors on commodity markets moving forward. At the end of 2007 it was estimated that a total of $175Bn was invested in commodity-linked assets (including commodity indexes). According to Barclays Capital, by the end of the second quarter of 2008 this figure had grown to $270B

n. But the turmoil in the financial markets and the collapse in the prices of most commodities together with a reduced appetite for risk and fund outflows have resulted in this figure dwindling to $154Bn by the end of 2008. And while many investors continue to withdraw their cash, some funds are also noting a willingness to re-invest. #### **WEEKLY COPPER EXCHANGE STOCKS AND CASH LME PRICE** kt $/tonne

_March 2009_ _Page 4_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ Based on our own outlook of the fundamentals, though, we believe that while the market should show an improvement towards the middle of this year, it will be rather short lived. Therefore, if investors are looking to get back into commodities in general and into copper specifically, their opportunities to do so will be minimal for now. At the heart of the issue is the ongoing challenging demand environment, which we expect will not show any sustained improvement until well into 2010. We should re-emphasise, therefore, that this current uptick in prices is a reflection of the Chinese SRB’s purchase programme rather than an indication of a wider industrial recovery. This may mean that, while the current actions of the SRB is benefitting the market in the short term, there is a danger that by artificially bolstering prices now, this will actually be detrimental to the market further out. The risk is that higher prices will deter companies from shutting down marginal mine capacity and that this will delay the turnaround in the market’s fortunes from one that is fundamentally in oversupply, to one where prices are buoyed in order to encourage additional supply developments. In this context recent evidence is clear in that there have been very few announced mine closures over the past month or so (see Production section). Perhaps even more worrying is the potential for companies that have already closed their mines under an earlier, lower price environment, to now hedge their production (27-month copper is currently trading at ~$4,100/t) and re-start their operations. At this price level more than 99% of mined copper production is profitable on a C1 cash cost basis! Furthermore, our current tally of mine closures indicates that the overall capacity lost to date is 750kt/a Cu which is by no means insignificant. Our supply/demand outlook for 2009 and 2010 remains largely unchanged from our February report. The headline reduction in LME stocks, though, which has prompted this month’s bullish move on prices, has meant that we have also had to revise our price upwards from $3313/t ($1.50/lb) last month to $3636/t ($1.65/lb) currently. ### CONSUMPTION _The debate about whether the fiscal stimulus packages will be enough to boost metals demand continues_ The near-term horizon for the global business environment has become even more uncertain as the fourth quarter 2008 economic indicators reflect far more damage to the macro economy than had been anticipated. The cessation in credit flows across major financial institutions since third quarter

2008 has caused a worldwide collapse in industrial output. The wave of fiscal stimulus packages across most developed economies will not be enough to offset the severe contraction in economic growth this year. In Europe, the remedies vary widely from Germany (current account surplus but fiscally conservative) to Spain (current account deficit and grappling with recession since first quarter 2008). The LDP party leadership in Japan is in severe turmoil and faces significant political opposition to the proposed stimulus packages. Meanwhile, in the USA, A US$789Bn stimulus package signed into law by President Obama will need to offset an estimated US$2 to 3Tn fiscal deficit over the next two years. This includes the US$460Bn deficit for the fiscal year ending October 2008. According to the Congressional Budget Office, the proposed bill could provide a boost to growth as early as second quarter 2009 and fiscal stimulus of US$170Bn by end-September 2009. But given the rate of economic deceleration, we remain cautious of meeting these milestones. _March 2009_ _Page 6_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ US BRASS MILL SHIPMENTS

With the USA representing the start of the worldwide economic collapse during 2008, it is no surprise that copper demand there has continued its decline in terms of global importance. Even so, it was not until late-Q1 2008 that the real spectre of a sustained decline in copper data became evident, as virtually all copper-consuming sectors could not withstand any longer the underlining message written by macro-economic collapse. As an example, from their recent peak of 128kt (metric - copper content) in March 2007, US brass mill shipments gradually tailed off over the course of the rest of that year, but still managed a reasonable 115kt in March 2008, according to data from the American Bureau of Statistics (ABMS). A typically strong September (100kt) seemed to defy the odds for another month, but the typically low December tally of just 59kt adequately summarised the degree of exhaustion in the sector, and compared poorly with the previous year’s end performance of 86kt. Equally, we saw a parallel performance from the copper wire rod sector, where production plunged to 79kt (metric) in December 2008 vs. 99kt a year prior, according to the ABMS. Meanwhile, shipments of copper wire rod by US mills to domestic customers fell by 9% year on year to 1.46Mt (metric), one third lower than at the start of this decade. In general, though, the single upside _nationally_ is that yearending inventories of wire rod in the USA fell by 10.7% from December 2007’s 25.4kt (metric), thereby slightly outstripping the rate of decline in apparent rod demand. _Coleman Cables suggests a near 30% decline in OEM business_ _Asarco finds a buyer in Vedanta – promptly puts Amarillo and Hayden on reduced work schedule_ _US copper demand expecting to decline further this year…_ _..and the same goes for Europe…_ _Italian semis sector contracted by almost 20% last quarter…_ The poor market conditions brought even further contraction and rationalisation to the industry, following similar efforts in 2007. One more indication regarding how poor the final quarter of last year was came with data released by Coleman Cables, which showed a near 30% collapse in cables shipped (in terms of Cu content) to the OEM sector compared with the prior quarter. Following on from the Q4 closure of FMI/PD’s 120kt Hawthorne rod mill near Chicago and with three other companies either closing or embarking on restructuring efforts at downstream facilities (such as winding/magnet wire), we expect that there will be some downtime, potentially further restructuring, ahead. Earlier this month, Indian producer Vedanta bought the assets of Asarco, and promptly announced “periodic slowdowns” of the Amarillo, TX refinery, rod mill and associated facilities during April. Asarco had already idled Amarillo’s rod and cake plants for one week at the start of this month. Effectively, it appears that all shifts have been cut back by 20% “as a response to market conditions”. However, across the company at Hayden, other changes to work patterns in place until June will likely affect Amarillo’s schedule also until then. All told, we believe that US copper demand overall fell away by 8.4% during 2008 to just over 2Mt, a level last seen in 1986-1987. Indeed, this year, we expect ongoing contraction of close to 10%, to 1.8Mt. With national economic confidence remaining low, there is little expectation for a recovery in industrial production and copper demand until 2011. In Europe, the effect of the financial crisis on economic activity is now reaching beyond just the economies with overheated property markets. German manufacturing exports have fallen off sharply with the contraction in regional trade flows; gross output will decline 2.7% this year. The UK, Spain and Italy will be hit hardest this year. Contraction in 2009 across the major European countries varies from 2.4%

to 4.1% decline (Belgium, Netherlands, and France) to 2.9% to 4.1% decline (Italy, Spain, Germany, and the UK). Romania and Hungary will see the sharpest contraction in the range of 3.3% to 4.8%, whilst Poland should be relatively less impacted with stagnant growth. The Baltic States of Latvia and Estonia were already weakening at the onset of the crisis and the marked deterioration in the Russian economy since third quarter 2008 will exacerbate the contraction. European copper demand contracted for a second consecutive year in 2008 under the strains of economic recession, after price volatility had prompted increased substitution during 2007. Last year’s estimated demand of 3.43Mt was over 15% down on 2000’s record level of 4.04Mt, with all countries except Spain contributing to the decline; our Spanish demand estimate of 300kt ( _vs._ 280kt for 2007) may yet be revised down given that final quarter figures, which were so poor elsewhere, require confirmation. Italian semis production figures show what the Spanish copper sector may have endured during the final quarter. Data from the national association, Assomet, reveal a near 22% yearon-year decline in production of semis for that period (-19.6% in pure copper semis and 22.3% down in alloy products), leaving total output down for the year by 12.2% at 1.19Mt. Italian demand for copper slid by a further 15.2% last year to just 650kt, putting it back to levels last seen in 1999. _March 2009_ _Page 8_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ ITALIAN SEMIS OUTPUT

In France, refined copper consumption fell in 2007 by 19.7% to 410kt largely because Nexans moved away from buying excess cathode to produce copper wire rod for the custom market. Last year we estimate this fell away by a further 6-7% due to the general economic decline, especially during the final quarter. December’s shipments of copper wire fell by 32.6% on the same month in 2007, to 15.9kt, while bar and shapes shipments fell by over 9% to 6.3kt. Meanwhile, overall production of copper semis by the year’s end stood at just 28% of its 2000 level at c.445kt. In Asia, the Japanese economy has lacked a domestic demand engine for some time now, leaving the economy dependent on exports for growth. However, Japan’s export market has been devastated by the appreciation of the yen while domestic demand has been destroyed by the marked slowdown in the auto, housing and electrical and electronic sectors from October last year. Actual automotive _production_ levels continued reasonably strongly through to Q3, but outstripped _sales_ , thereby leaving a backlog that will need to be drawn down before new manufacturing can begin. The Japan Automobile Manufacturers’ projection that car sales

will fall by 4.5% in 2009 is compounded by its forecast that domestic new car sales will fall by 4.9%, dropping below 5M units for the first time in 30 years. All recent measures of economic activity reflect a dramatic descent into recession. We expect demand to contract by 6.0% this year and remain very weak over the medium term because of the high level of government debt and rising social security obligations. The two principal semis production sectors continue to decline under the collapse of the mainstay sectors such as housing/construction and automobile sales. According to the Japan Copper and Brass Association the output of copper and alloy products fell by 5.9% last year, following the 4.2% decline recorded in 2007, and January output at 43.4kt, was 43% down on the prior year. Meanwhile, the Japanese Electric Wire and Cable Makers’ Association reported a 4.9% decline in shipments in 2008, following the 1.6% drop during 2007, with first-month 2009 figures down by 22%. In this light, as recently as January we deemed it necessary to reduce our 2009 copper demand forecasts for the country to c.1Mt, which would represent a drop of almost 17% on 2008’s 1.2Mt. We learned that orders began the year down 50% on business levels of 12 months prior, with many brass mills operating at only 10% of capacity and wire rod producers operating at between 50-60% of capacity. _Chinese statistics fan interpretation rather than facts…_ _..refined Cu imports up, but others all down_ In China, the usual mйlange of production and trade data to which all interested parties refer has served only to stoke the fires under the debate regarding the commencement and extent of purchases of refined copper by the State Reserve Board (SRB). In short, there is a disconnect between using bald statistics alone and attempting to determine an appropriate apparent refined copper demand figure. While this is clearly nothing new, the _active_ involvement by the SRB in copper imports this year is matched by a commensurate shortage of the facts and, consequently, it

is still too soon to gauge with any degree of accuracy the real level of Chinese copper demand. 

Data from the CNIA show refined copper imports up by 71.5% for the first two months of this year, to 451kt.  But this is the only recorded increase in copperrelated items: scrap imports were down by 50% (other intermediates, such as matte, blister and anode were similarly down), semis imports were down 18%.

As was the case in January, copper concentrate imports into China during February, at 445kdmt, were almost flat (+0.2%) on the same period in 2008. This brings the year-to-date figure to 950kdmt.  Chile, with a cumulative market share of 21%, remains ahead of Peru (18.4%), followed by Australia (14.4%). Further incentives to boost concentrate imports are under active consideration. We hear, for example, that China’s State Council is considering reintroducing the refunding of VAT (currently 17%) that is paid on imported copper raw materials including concentrates.  This practice was first introduced (retroactively to 2000) during 2001 when a number of the larger copper smelters were granted rebates on 100% of the 13% VAT paid on imported concentrates up to an overall import total of 800kt/a.  This was maintained in 2001 and 2002 and then amended to a 30% rebate in 2003 covering 1.2Mt/a (with the remaining 70% allocated to a pool to fund overseas mining acquisitions) which remained in place through 2005, after which the rebate was removed. 

China’s appetite for developing new copper smelting and refining capacity appears far from diminished despite the recent global economic turmoil.  During March there have been announcements regarding three greenfield projects that are in varying stages of development.  Jiangxi Shangrao Huasheng Nonferrous Metals Co. Ltd reported the production of its first batch of blister copper on February 26<sup>th</sup> .  The operation is a joint venture between Jiangxi Tungsten Group and Huafeng Copper Co. Ltd.  At capacity the plant will be capable of producing 40kt/a of blister along with nickel sulphate (5kt/a) and zinc sulphate (2kt/a). Elsewhere, Zinjin Copper Co. held an inauguration ceremony on March 11<sup>th</sup> to initiate (presumably groundbreaking of) its 200kt/a smelter/refinery project in Fujian.  Capital costs are estimated a $380M with a construction time of 30 months.  The project will also produce 730kt/a of sulphuric acid as well as 4.5t/a of gold and 113t/a of silver.  Raw materials will be sourced from the Zijin

shan mine as well as from overseas. Finally, Chifeng Fubang Copper Co., located in Inner Mongolia, is progressing with the construction of its 100kt/a copper smelter project with trial production scheduled for October 2009. Fubang Copper is owned by Guangdong Qiaoxing Group which is investing $80M in the project. Plans also call for the addition of a 100kt/a refinery at a later date. shortage of No. 2 scrap resulted in a further, albeit temporary, narrowing of the price spreads in the US market, from 12c/lb under May Comex last month to 10c/lb in mid March. By month end, however, spreads had widened back to February’s level of 12c/lb. Interestingly, Chinese scrap demand would be even higher currently were it not for the increase in buyers’ deposit rates which are now 70% compared with 30% last year. The reason for the increase has been to protect overseas scrap sellers from potential defaults (as occurred when prices fell dramatically last year). By comparison, the margins required for copper cathode purchase LCs are currently closer to 20-30%. US copper producer Asarco has signed a revised agreement to sell most of its operating assets to Vedanta subsidiary Sterlite (USA).  The new deal involves a cash payment of $1.1Bn plus a promissory note for $600M payable over nine years.  This is a considerable decline from the original bid of $2.6Bn which was on offer in May 2008 when copper prices were considerably higher than today’s levels.  Last year Asarco’s two open pit mining/milling operations produced 128kt of copper-in-concentrate while output of refined copper totalled 238kt including 181kt from the Amarillo tankhouse and 57kt from the Ray and Silver Bell SxEw operations.  Asarco recently announced that it was initiating periodic curtailments at its Amarillo rod and cake plants due to depressed market conditions (see Consumption section). 

Production from the Lady Annie SxEw mine in Queensland, Australia has been suspended after flooding that occurred during February.  Copper Co., the mine’s owners, has been in receivership since the end of 2008 and the receivers have decided that an indefinite suspension of the operation is the most appropriate action to maximise returns for shareholders.  Lady Annie was commissioned in late 2007 and produced ~15kt of SxEw cathode in 2008. 

African Copper’s Mowana mine in Botswana could receive a new lease of life after Natasa Mining offered to rescue the troubled producer in exchange for a majority shareholding.  The deal would involve Natasa providing a $16.5M cash injection into African Copper.  Natasa is expected to

review the options for Mowana including plans to expand the operation beyond its 25kt/a Cu capacity. The project was commissioned in January 2008 but only reached commercial production in October. The sharp decline in copper prices, coupled with various operating difficulties, forced African Copper to close the mine in January 2009. Germany’s Aurubis (formerly Norddeutsche Affinerie) is to expand production at its Hamburg smelting/refining complex, raising cathode output from 380kt/a to 415kt/a in 2011 at an estimated cost of $64M. As part of this programme, smelter throughput is to be increased from 1.1Mt/a to 1.25Mt/a during a routine maintenance shutdown of the plant between September and October 2011. Last year the company announced that it was embarking upon an $80M scrap recycling expansion initiative at its Luenen secondary smelter/refinery that would include the installation of a second KRS furnace as well as equipment to reduce waste gas emissions. Overall feed processing capacity will increase from 220kt/a to 350kt/a by 2011. Indonesia’s PT Aneka Tambang is considering plans to build a greenfield custom copper smelter/refinery complex in response to the country’s drive to ban copper concentrate exports from 2014. While the scale of the complex is not known at the present time it could be similar in size to Gresik, i.e. 270-300kt/a Cu.
